evidence_records.technical_detail: NTRS 20260005612 (2026 abstract/poster): photoelectric and ionization detectors, an aerosol sensor and a combustion-product monitor exposed to fabric smoke in the GASP chamber; for the materials studied the ionization detector gave the earliest signal. Discrimination work is ongoing.
limitations: Development status report; no discrimination performance reported yet.
evidence_records.anchor_quote: smoke and real lunar dust have overlapping particle sizes that set off the detector
evidence_records.source_title: Early Fire Detection System for Partial and Low Gravity Environments

evidence_records.hardware_family: Cygnus cargo vehicle (Saffire Far Field Diagnostics)
evidence_records.detector: assumed 2 mg/m3 alarm point applied to DustTrak DRX aerosol mass at the Far Field Diagnostics
evidence_records.statement: In the 2026 Saffire VI results, an assumed 2 mg/m3 smoke alarm point would have been reached only after carbon monoxide had already exceeded the 24-hour exposure limit in both PMMA fires, which burned at about 30% oxygen and reduced pressure.
evidence_records.technical_detail: Urban et al. (2026, NTRS 20260001992), Table 1 and alarm-threshold discussion: Saffire VI PMMA tests at 544 and 550 mbar with O2 mole fractions 0.30 and 0.29 reached 2 mg/m3 at 1037 s and 1603 s, when CO had risen 105 and 283 ppm (24-h SMAC 100 ppm). Flaming fires in an uncrewed Cygnus; the authors conclude a lower threshold or more detectors would be needed for that configuration.
limitations: Assumed alarm threshold, not a spacecraft detector's actual alarm.
Flaming fires in one vehicle geometry; two tests.
Not pyrolysis smoke.

evidence_records.hardware_family: Cygnus cargo vehicle (Saffire Far Field Diagnostics)
evidence_records.detector: ionization sensor from a commercial smoke detector and DustTrak DRX (Far Field Diagnostics)
evidence_records.statement: Saffire IV-VI burned PMMA, SIBAL and cotton samples in seven large low-gravity fires with cabin oxygen and pressure moved toward exploration atmospheres, while measuring smoke aerosol and gases at the Far Field Diagnostics.
evidence_records.technical_detail: Urban et al. (2026, NTRS 20260001992): O2 mole fraction 0.22-0.31, pressure 541-1000 mbar; the FFD held CO/CO2/O2 sensors, an ionization sensor from a commercial smoke detector and a DustTrak DRX. These are flaming fires; no spacecraft smoke detector (ISS or Shuttle type) was evaluated.
limitations: Flaming fires; commercial ionization sensor and aerosol monitor only.

evidence_records.detector: heritage spacecraft smoke detectors (Shuttle ionization, ISS photoelectric)
evidence_records.statement: A 2025 NASA paper states that high sensitivity to the earliest smoke and immunity to dusty events cannot both be achieved with the smoke detectors currently used in space vehicles.
evidence_records.technical_detail: ICES 2025 paper on dust-tolerant smoke detection: both heritage technologies are particle detectors that cannot tell smoke from dust, and the authors conclude that dust-tolerant detectors are needed for exploration.
limitations: Review/position statement.
evidence_records.anchor_quote: these two goals are mutually exclusive and cannot be achieved simultaneously
evidence_records.source_title: Towards Dust-tolerant Smoke Detection in Future Space Missions

evidence_records.hardware_family: spacecraft cabins (operational history)
evidence_records.statement: The same 2025 paper states that historically most spacecraft smoke-alarm events have been caused by nuisance dust rather than smoke, but ISS incidents are not publicly tracked.
evidence_records.technical_detail: ICES 2025 dust-tolerant detection paper: Shuttle reports total 14 events combining built-in-test failures and false alarms; ISS evidence is anecdotal. No rate can be derived from the examined sources.
limitations: No public incident database; anecdotal for ISS.

evidence_records.statement: Polarimetric detector prototypes, which flag irregular dust by its depolarised scattered light, indicated smoke-versus-lunar-simulant discrimination in early tests reported in 2025.

limitations: Early laboratory results; not flight-qualified.

evidence_records.value_unit: psi (HALO nominal pressure; 70.3 kPa)
evidence_records.statement: Exploration habitats run below sea-level pressure (Gateway HALO nominally 10.2 psi); photoelectric detection is pressure-independent, but an ionization detector's baseline changes at low pressure and must be characterised.
evidence_records.technical_detail: ICES 2025 dust-tolerant detection paper (HALO nominal 10.2 psi / 70.3 kPa); hardware must also survive vacuum.
limitations: Need statement; no low-pressure detector test reported.

evidence_records.hardware_family: Gateway HALO module
evidence_records.statement: As of 2025 no NASA standard governs smoke-detector performance for space use, so the Gateway HALO alarm threshold had to be derived from tabulated 2012 ground tests of spacecraft materials including Kapton and Teflon.
evidence_records.technical_detail: ICES 2025 paper on the HALO smoke-detector threshold; the authors list data limitations (single 0.5 g samples, no time-resolved data, unrepeatable smoke generation) and recommend new campaigns with multiple low-pressure test points.
limitations: Threshold analysis, not a detector test.
evidence_records.derived_from: 2012 GRC tests at WSTF with 0.5 g samples

evidence_records.hardware_family: ISS, Orion, HLS, Gateway
evidence_records.detector: Anomaly Gas Analyzer (laser spectroscopy: CO, HCN, HF, HCl, CO2, O2 and others)
evidence_records.statement: Gas sensing has advanced: the Anomaly Gas Analyzer, which monitors combustion gases such as CO, HCN, HF and HCl, is deployed on the ISS, flew on Artemis 2 and is being built for the lunar lander.
evidence_records.technical_detail: NTRS 20260003174 (2026): seven units on ISS, Orion units, HLS engineering units delivered in 2025, and a constituent-monitor subset for Gateway HALO. It is a contingency air monitor, not a smoke detector.
limitations: Gas monitor; does not address particle-based smoke detection.

research_gaps.topic: Smoke production, transport and detection in lunar (partial) gravity
research_gaps.rule: no detector-evaluating investigation profile at lunar/partial gravity
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, no smoke-detector test or smoke-particle measurement was made in lunar or other partial gravity; the 2021 white paper lists the airflow dependence of particle size in lunar gravity as unknown, and a 2023 NASA study addressed detector placement only by simulation.
research_gaps.detail: Ground facilities give only seconds of lunar gravity (drop-tower centrifuge 5.2 s, parabolic flights about 30 s). Treating partial-gravity behaviour as bounded by microgravity and 1 g results is a hypothesis, not evidence, for smoke transport and detection.

research_gaps.topic: Controlled false-alarm testing of spacecraft smoke detectors with cabin and lunar dust
research_gaps.rule: no false_alarm record that comes from a controlled, directly observed test
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, no controlled test measures how often the ISS or Shuttle smoke detector false-alarms on cabin dust or lunar dust; false alarms are documented only as operational reports, and dust-discriminating detectors exist only as early prototypes.
research_gaps.detail: False alarms (alarm without fire) are a different event from missed alarms. ISS background-aerosol data go back to DAFT; the 2025 dust-tolerant detector paper reports early polarimetric prototype results with a lunar simulant.

research_gaps.detail: SAME and SAME-R heated samples below ignition to emulate an overheat event. Saffire IV-VI fires were large flaming burns in an uncrewed Cygnus.

research_gaps.topic: ISS smoke-detector response to PMMA smoke
research_gaps.rule: material/detector pair not tested in microgravity with an alarm evaluation
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, the ISS smoke detector was never tested with PMMA smoke in microgravity and no alarm decision was evaluated for PMMA smoke; its only exposure was a single 1 g ground test that measured signal against smoke mass.
research_gaps.detail: Saffire IV-VI burned PMMA in microgravity but measured smoke with a commercial ionization sensor and an aerosol monitor, not with the ISS detector. Model A (BASS-II PMMA flame spread) says nothing about smoke-detector response.

research_gaps.topic: Smoke-detector response to lithium-ion battery smoke
research_gaps.rule: material not tested with any smoke detector in microgravity with an alarm evaluation
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, no spacecraft smoke-detector test with lithium-ion battery smoke was found, although laptop battery fires are named among the most likely long-mission fire scenarios.
research_gaps.detail: The 2021 white paper knew of only one study characterising laptop-scale battery smoke particles.

research_gaps.topic: Kapton and Teflon detector response differs between SAME (2007) and SAME-R (2010)
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, the ISS detector's response to Kapton and Teflon smoke differs strongly between the 2007 SAME and 2010 SAME-R campaigns, and no source explains why.
research_gaps.detail: Kapton reached 2.0 V in every SAME run but in a minority of SAME-R runs, while Teflon went the other way; the measured counts are in the cited records.

research_gaps.topic: Shuttle detector: 'strong signal in all tests' vs 'some runs below alarm boundary'
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, the 2010 SAME report and the 2018 paper disagree on whether the Space Shuttle ionization detector responded to all SAME smokes; the difference may come from test sets and criteria and is unresolved.

research_gaps.topic: Size increase of zero-flow smoke reported with different magnitudes
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, the zero-flow particle-size increase is reported as 30 % to 40 %, as 2 to 3 times and as 1.7 times on average; the direction agrees but the magnitude is unresolved.

research_gaps.topic: Unaged Teflon row of the 2012 SAME-2 particle-size table is internally inconsistent
research_gaps.statement: Within the examined sources, the unaged Teflon row of the 2012 particle-size table cannot be reproduced from its own geometric values; separate averaging of each statistic is a likely but undocumented cause.

scientific_comparisons.statement: The published no-alarm statements and Model C's 2.0 V fractions must not be combined: the 2018 and 2021 documents describe ISS-detector alarm behaviour in the SAME tests without denominators, while Model C counts SAME plus SAME-R primary runs whose measured scatter reached a derived 2.0 V level.
scientific_comparisons.detail: Side by side, Kapton stayed below 2.0 V in 12 of 21 primary runs and Teflon in 11 of 15, but the definitions (alarm behaviour vs a threshold label), test sets (SAME vs SAME + SAME-R) and denominators differ, so neither result confirms or refutes the other numerically.

scientific_comparisons.title: From experimental limitation to open technology need
scientific_comparisons.statement: The 2018 experiments showed that spacecraft detectors missed small-particle smokes; the 2021 white paper turned this into research questions on fuels, gravity, exploration atmospheres and multi-sensor detection; the 2025 SBIR call still lists selective, multi-property sensing as an open need and still reports frequent ISS false alarms.
scientific_comparisons.detail: 2026 follow-up work (dust-tolerant prototypes, the Saffire IV-VI time-to-alarm analysis, gas analyzers) addresses parts of these needs, but within the examined sources none closes the Kapton/Teflon or partial-gravity questions. The 2026 status is limited to the documents found and is not exhaustive.

stages.label: Experiment reports (SAME 2010, SAME-R 2014)
stages.summary: Flight data show small Kapton/Teflon particles and erratic light-scattering response; the team already calls for dust-immune detection for lunar missions and demonstrates a two-moment prototype.

stages.label: Experimental limitation (NASA/NIST)
stages.summary: Neither spacecraft detector sensed every smoke; the ISS detector would not have alarmed for over half of Kapton and about two thirds of Teflon tests.

stages.label: Research questions (decadal white paper)
stages.summary: Restates the SAME result and asks how fuels, lunar gravity and exploration atmospheres change fire signatures; proposes multi-sensor networks.

stages.label: Open technology needs (SBIR, ICES)
stages.summary: Selective, multi-property, small-particle sensing for reduced-pressure, elevated-O2 habitats; frequent ISS false alarms; no NASA smoke-detector performance standard.

stages.label: Status in reachable sources
stages.summary: Partial-gravity detector development at NASA Glenn, Saffire IV-VI time-to-alarm results at exploration-like atmospheres, deployed gas analyzers; not an exhaustive survey.
